title: Sawan Somwar Is Here: Build a Satisfying Vrat Thali Without Onion or Garlic
excerpt: The holy month of Shravan is underway, and today marks the first Monday fast. Here's how to put together a complete fasting thali anchored by a rich, no-onion paneer masala.
body:
• Sawan 2026 runs from July 30 to August 28; the first Sawan Somwar falls on August 3
  • Vrat rules prohibit onion, garlic, wheat, and regular salt — but paneer, dairy, sabudana, and vrat-friendly flours are all fair game
  • A cashew-tomato-based paneer masala without onion or garlic makes a protein-rich centerpiece for any fasting thali

The monsoon has arrived, and with it the month of Shravan — the holiest stretch in the Hindu calendar and the one most closely tied to Lord Shiva. Today, August 3, is the first of four Sawan Somwar fasts in 2026, with the remaining three falling on August 10, 17, and 24. For millions of devotees across India and the diaspora, that means weeks of careful meal planning around a strict set of fasting rules.

The good news: a Sawan vrat thali can be far more interesting than boiled potatoes and fruit. At its center, a no-onion, no-garlic paneer masala — rich with cashew paste, tomatoes, and whole spices — delivers the kind of satisfying, protein-packed dish that makes fasting feel less like deprivation and more like a culinary challenge worth taking on.

What You Can and Cannot Eat

Sawan fasting follows a well-defined pantry. According to Zoff Foods and other guides to Shravan vrat cooking, the permitted ingredients include vrat-friendly flours like kuttu (buckwheat), singhara (water chestnut), and rajgira (amaranth); sabudana (tapioca pearls); samak rice (barnyard millet); and vegetables such as potato, sweet potato, arbi, bottle gourd, pumpkin, and raw banana. All dairy — milk, curd, paneer, ghee — is welcome. Makhana, dry fruits, and peanuts round out the snacking options.

"For millions of devotees across India and the diaspora, that means weeks of careful meal planning around a strict set of fasting rules."

What's off the table: wheat, rice, lentils, besan, regular table salt (rock salt or sendha namak is used instead), and — crucially — onion and garlic. The spice rack is pared down to cumin, black pepper, green cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, fresh ginger, and green chilli.

For the Diaspora Kitchen

Indian families abroad often find Sawan fasting easier than expected. Paneer is widely available in South Asian grocery stores across the U.S., U.K., Canada, and the Middle East, and kuttu and singhara flours have become staples in the international aisle. Samak rice can be harder to source — barnyard millet, available at health food stores, is the same grain under a different name. Rock salt (sendha namak) is sold as Himalayan pink salt in most Western supermarkets, making the swap straightforward.

The deeper challenge is time. Vrat cooking relies on fresh preparation — no pre-made curry pastes, no shortcut spice blends with onion powder lurking in the ingredients list. For working families juggling fast days with school runs and office hours, batch-prepping the cashew-tomato base on a weekend and freezing it in portions can save 15-20 minutes on a Monday morning.

What's Next

The second Sawan Somwar falls on August 10, followed by the third on August 17. The month wraps up on August 28 with Sawan Purnima, which coincides with Raksha Bandhan this year. Each Monday brings a fresh opportunity to experiment with the vrat pantry — try swapping the paneer masala for a pumpkin bharta one week, or a raw banana tikki the next. The constraints of fasting have always been, at their best, an invitation to creativity in the kitchen.
